I never say the number first. A price with nothing beside it is just a big number, and if you do not give the customer a comparison, they will find their own, and it will be the cheapest thing they can remember. So the sentence before the price is always the comparison: what they spend today, what the problem costs them every month, or what the other option costs over three years. The second habit is breaking it down. Almost everything that looks expensive turns out to be three things, and only one of them is actually being argued about, and once it is on the table in parts, the conversation gets much smaller. And here is a small thing that costs people deals. If you hesitate while you are saying a number, the customer does not hear somebody thinking in a second language. They hear doubt about the price, and then you are negotiating a figure that you yourself have already admitted is too high.

When three quotes land on my desk, people assume I compare them with each other. I do not, or at least not first. My real benchmark is what we pay today, and that number includes the people, which most vendors forget. If your proposal is more expensive than the tool we have and cheaper than the tool plus the two people, then we have something to talk about. If a quote arrives as one number with nothing underneath it, I send it back and ask for a breakdown, and I will tell you honestly what I have learned from doing that for years: the ones who cannot break it down usually cannot defend it either. And the fastest way to lose me is the discount that arrives too early. If fifteen per cent appears before I have even pushed, then the first price was not real, and now I have to check every other number in the document twice.
